overview.text: Treblinka II was a Nazi killing center in German-occupied Poland, established near the separate Treblinka I forced-labor camp. It opened in July 1942 as part of Operation Reinhard, the German campaign to murder Jews in occupied Poland. Trains brought people from the Warsaw ghetto and other areas; perpetrators killed most arrivals in gas chambers using engine exhaust. Hundreds of thousands of Jews were murdered there, along with members of other persecuted groups. Jewish prisoners organized an uprising on August 2, 1943, and some escaped. The Germans then dismantled the killing center and tried to hide evidence of their crimes. The two Treblinka camps had different functions and closure dates.

Treblinka I was a separate forced-labor camp.
The first transport to Treblinka II came from the Warsaw ghetto in July 1942.
Prisoners revolted on August 2, 1943.
The Nazis dismantled Treblinka II later in 1943.

overview.text: The Stahlhelm was a German steel combat helmet introduced during World War I. Its 1916 model replaced headgear such as the leather spiked Pickelhaube, which offered little protection against shell fragments and shrapnel. The Stahlhelm's deep sides helped shield soldiers' ears and necks while leaving room to see ahead. British soldiers nicknamed its distinctive profile the “coal scuttle.” Early helmets were field gray, but reflective paint made wearers conspicuous. In July 1918 German command ordered matte, multicolor camouflage patterns that soldiers often painted themselves. Later versions changed details while retaining the recognizable basic outline. The helmet became a visual symbol of German soldiers across the two world wars.

Its shell helped protect the neck and ears.
British soldiers called its shape the “coal scuttle.”

overview.text: Pliny the Elder was a Roman writer, scholar and naval commander whose surviving work, Natural History, gathered information on plants, animals, minerals, art and many other subjects. Its 37 books became an influential model for later encyclopedias, although many ancient claims were not experimentally checked. In 79 CE Pliny commanded the fleet at Misenum when Mount Vesuvius erupted. His nephew, Pliny the Younger, wrote that Pliny first wanted to observe the eruption, then took ships toward the threatened coast to help people escape. He reached Stabiae but died there amid the disaster. The nephew's letters to Tacitus are the principal ancient account of his final journey.

overview.text: A political assassination is the deliberate killing of a prominent person whose public role, the attacker's motive, or the killing's political consequences give the act political significance. An unsuccessful attack is an assassination attempt. Targets can include rulers, candidates and other public figures, and motives differ: ideology, grievances, personal obsession and organized conspiracies all appear in historical records. Abraham Lincoln was killed by Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth in 1865, while President John F. Kennedy was killed in Dallas in 1963; investigators did not establish the same kind of motive in every case. Such violence can alter leadership and trigger lasting public debate about security, responsibility and political conflict.

An official inquiry listed the motive in Kennedy’s case as unknown.

overview.text: Cecil Rhodes was a British mining magnate and imperial politician in southern Africa. He built a fortune from Kimberley diamonds and created De Beers Consolidated Mines in 1888. As prime minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896, he backed laws that restricted Black Africans' landholding and voting rights. He also directed the British South Africa Company, whose expansion helped colonize territory in what are now Zimbabwe and neighboring regions. Rhodes resigned after supporting the failed Jameson Raid against the South African Republic. His will funded scholarships at Oxford, while his colonial policies and racial views have made his public monuments intensely contested. His wealth and political power were closely connected.

overview.text: India's Emergency was a nationwide suspension of normal democratic protections from June 1975 to March 1977 under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The government cited internal instability and used emergency powers to detain opponents, limit civil liberties and censor newspapers. Many journalists faced pressure or arrest, while some newspapers protested with blank editorials. A family-planning campaign included coerced sterilizations, particularly as pressure to meet official goals intensified. When elections were held in March 1977, Gandhi's Congress party lost and the Emergency was lifted. A later inquiry, the Shah Commission, investigated abuses. The period remains an important example of how constitutional emergency powers can be used to concentrate authority.

overview.text: A turtle ship, or geobukseon, was a Korean warship associated with Admiral Yi Sun-sin's naval defense during Japan's invasions of Joseon Korea in the 1590s. It adapted a larger Korean fighting ship with a covered upper deck shaped like a turtle's back. Historical descriptions say spikes or blades discouraged enemy sailors from boarding, while openings allowed the crew to fire cannon in several directions. Yi and his officers refined an earlier Korean shipbuilding idea rather than inventing the concept from nothing. Although turtle ships became famous symbols of Korean resistance, their exact construction remains debated. In particular, historians have not established that their roofs were fully clad in iron.

overview.text: Gaelic can refer to a branch of Celtic languages and to cultural traditions connected with their speakers. Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx belong to the Goidelic, or Gaelic, branch; Welsh, Breton and Cornish belong to a different Celtic branch. Irish and Scottish Gaelic are related but are distinct modern languages. In Ireland, the late nineteenth-century Gaelic Revival sought to strengthen the Irish language and traditional literature, music and other arts. Douglas Hyde chaired the Gaelic League's founding meeting in 1893 and became its first president. The League organized classes and cultural events. Its original purpose was cultural and nonsectarian, though some participants later took part in Irish nationalist politics.

overview.text: The Cilician pirates were maritime raiders associated with Cilicia, a region on the southern coast of present-day Turkey, during the late Roman Republic. Their crews were not all necessarily from Cilicia. They attacked ships and coastal communities, seized captives for ransom or sale, and disrupted Mediterranean travel and trade. Ancient author Plutarch describes Cilicia as an early base and reports that pirates captured a young Julius Caesar near the island of Pharmacusa; his colorful details should be read as an ancient account, not a transcript. Rome gave Pompey a large command against the pirates in 67 BCE. His campaign culminated in their defeat near Coracesium, sharply reducing their power without ending Mediterranean piracy forever.

overview.text: The Olmec civilization flourished along the Gulf Coast of what is now Mexico during the early history of Mesoamerica. Its major centers included San Lorenzo in Veracruz and La Venta in Tabasco. San Lorenzo's inhabitants reshaped their landscape into terraces and transported volcanic stone from the Tuxtla Mountains to carve monumental thrones and heads. La Venta later became an important ceremonial center, with four colossal heads, greenstone offerings and a large earthen pyramid. INAH describes the heads as male figures bearing symbols of power. Archaeologists interpret the monuments as signs of elite status, although the identities of the people portrayed are unknown. These sites also reveal farming, trade and complex social organization beyond the famous sculptures.
